CausalChain: Cancer cell stress (hypoxia, oxidative stress) -> generation of specific tRFs -> selective loading of tRFs into exosomes -> exosome secretion and uptake by tumor-associated macrophages -> tRFs interact with macrophage RNA-binding proteins (e.g., YBX1) -> altered cytokine mRNA translation -> shift in macrophage polarization toward an M2-like, immunosuppressive phenotype -> enhanced tumor progression
Hypothesis: Exosome-mediated transfer of cancer-derived tRNA-derived fragments reprograms tumor-associated macrophages by altering cytokine translation, leading to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that promotes cancer progression.
Abstract: Recent studies of tRNA‐derived fragments (tRFs) have revealed their multifaceted roles in cancer cellular phenotypes, including the regulation of mRNA stability, modulation of protein translation, and response to cellular stress. Building on these observations, we propose that tRFs secreted in exosomes from cancer cells modulate the function of tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) in the hypoxic tumor microenvironment. In our hypothesis, stress‐induced cancer cells generate specific tRF species, which are preferentially loaded into exosomes and transferred to neighboring TAMs. Upon uptake, these tRFs interact with key RNA binding proteins (such as YBX1) that regulate cytokine mRNA translation, thereby influencing macrophage polarization toward a pro‐tumoral immunosuppressive (M2‐like) phenotype. This horizontal transfer mechanism would enable cancer cells to indirectly shape surrounding immune cell functions, promoting an environment that favors tumor progression. Our hypothesis, if validated, could provide novel insights into intercellular communication in the tumor microenvironment and highlight new therapeutic targets against cancer.
